extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature (scientists, researchers, university/industry practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and reporting on scientific work (laboratory/field studies, apparatus papers, institutional reports) for a scientific-news or journal audience, focusing on methods, significance, and utility. Emphasises appraisal of experimental method, practical value, and institutional/educational arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate practical value relative to effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgements should consider whether the labour expended on a line of work is justified by its value (e.g. 'we are inclined to be sceptical as to whether the value of such work is equal to the labour expended upon it').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should weigh the amount of trouble taken against demonstrated outcomes or utility; lack of clear beneficial outcome (for example, 'the value of "interfering" with the natural reproduction of the food-fishes still remains to be proved') is a reason for scepticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoroughness and careful observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Work that 'illustrates his capacity for taking pains' and 'has gone more carefully into detail' is positively characterised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give credit for painstaking, detailed observational work and for analyses that go into finer detail than prior treatments; value increases when such work can be compared and shown consistent with other investigators' observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration with independent studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare results with other investigators (e.g. 'his observations on this point agree well with those of Mr. R. A. Todd on the same species in the North Sea').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A study gains credibility when its findings are consonant with independent work; reviewers should note agreement/disagreement with contemporaneous studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of irregularity and limits of generalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Report and interpret observed variability (e.g. fish movements 'appear to be irregular according to present knowledge').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-generalising from irregular or sparse observations; explicitly state when patterns are irregular or when data do not support a simple universal conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include applied/intervention studies where relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: When addressing pollution or remediation (e.g. 'sewage pollution of shell-fish') include experimental work on purification or remedy (the reviewer regrets absence of a report on 'the action of copper in connection with the purification of infected shell-fish').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a problem has an applied dimension, expect or request experiments testing remediation measures as part of a complete report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use suitable, validated purification and analytical methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for methods demonstrated to be 'suitable and satisfactory' for separating and purifying elements (e.g. Ekman's and Petterson's method for purification of selenium).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the chosen purification procedure in detail; where available use established methods and state their suitability and limitations (possible exceptions, e.g. mercury, tellurium, arsenic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Report detection limits and use check/blank trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantify analytical limits and check for trace contaminants (e.g. sublimate contains 'certainly less than one-tenth per cent. of tellurium, and probably less than one-fortieth per cent.'; tests for arsenic with 'constant reference to check and blank trials').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should give numerical estimates of trace impurities, describe limits of detection, and report use of blank/check trials to validate results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge methodological uncertainties and avoid overreach
rubrics_metrics.description: Where perfect separation or absolute criteria are lacking (e.g. 'there does not seem to be any perfectly satisfactory criterion as to the complete absence of dioxide') the investigator should acknowledge remaining uncertainties and not proceed to unwarranted conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should expect candid discussion of limitations and should not fault authors for reasonable caution where methods cannot fully resolve an issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design experiments to discriminate between competing theories
rubrics_metrics.description: When theories compete (e.g. whether mantle light is 'mere thermal radiation' or involves 'catalysis' by ceria), provide experiments capable of distinguishing mechanisms (e.g. Rubens' optical experiment showing apparent colour change when heated; tests comparing behaviour of ceria vs zirconia mantles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical tests should target contrasting predictions of rival hypotheses; include control cases and note possible alternative explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider instrumentation limitations when reporting temperatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Thermocouple readings may be 'far too low' because the thermocouple 'never reaches the real temperature of the flame'; thus interpretation must account for instrument bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should discuss measurement limitations and how they affect conclusions (e.g., whether flame temperature is underestimated) and consider alternative measurement approaches or corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance emissivity and heat-transfer in lamp/mantle design
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical guidance: mantle threads must be fine so the flame can rush through meshes; emissivity affects temperature and light output (increasing emissivity can increase total radiation but lower temperature, altering light vs heat proportion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design choices (mesh fineness, emissivity, draught arrangements such as 'the intensive system') should be justified by their effect on heat flow and luminous efficiency; explain trade-offs (whiteness → higher temperature but low emissivity → less light; darkness → more total radiation but cooler mantle → redder, less useful light).

rubrics_metrics.name: Report practical apparatus improvements and safety/convenience features
rubrics_metrics.description: When describing applied devices (e.g. gas burner ignition mechanisms or pilot-jet systems), include their operational advantages (e.g. letting one main tap light multiple burners) and how they overcome drawbacks (e.g. eliminating a continuously burning jet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe mechanical or control attachments, explain their function, and note improvements in convenience and safety for users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify materials, operating conditions, and circuit considerations for electric lamps
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss filament materials (tungsten, osmium, tantalum, zircon/tungsten compounds), voltage ratings (100–200 V), and behaviour under alternating vs direct current (e.g. 'tantalum... will not last long on alternating currents'; microstructural changes observed after running).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers on lamp technology should state conductor composition, intended voltage, efficiency claims, observed failure modes for different circuits, and mechanical design features (e.g. multiple loops, light springs to keep loops taut).

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial/works chemist: curriculum and practical competence
rubrics_metrics.description: To train a works chemist properly: 'he ought to go to college better prepared, and have at least four years of study, with more mechanics and physics in the beginning and a proper course of chemical technology in the end.' Also emphasise that a works chemist is 'not solely an analyst, but a highly useful practical technologist'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational programs should include extended study (≈4 years), stronger mechanics and physics early on, and applied chemical-technology training later; industry should trust trained works chemists with practical responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial practice standards: plant planning and operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Works chemist responsibilities include site selection, disposition of buildings and plant, erection of power-houses, provision for smoke prevention, automatic stokers, water softeners, feed-water heaters, and general engineering details affecting economy and production control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors reporting on industrial chemistry should address engineering, safety, and process-economy considerations—not merely laboratory-scale operations 'writ large'—and describe practical installations and mitigations of risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diploma awarding criteria in anthropology at Cambridge (procedural standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation: a diploma in anthropology be established; an advanced student who has studied under the board and 'has presented a thesis, which thesis has been approved for a certificate of research, shall... be entitled to a diploma... on the payment of such fees as the Senate may... determine.' Also former graduates who have presented an approved thesis may claim the diploma on payment of fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal recognition (diploma) should be contingent on supervised study, presentation of an approved thesis, and fulfilment of administrative conditions (fees).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation practice for society talks
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective presentations 'trace the efforts of previous observers', provide enlarged figures drawn on the board to illustrate interpretations, and include photographic or specimen exhibits when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speakers should contextualise work historically, include clear visual aids (figures, photographs, specimens), and demonstrate how their observations relate to prior interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit experimental data to simple empirical laws where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: In studies of conduction on heating salts the relation between saturation-current and absolute temperature was represented 'with fair accuracy' by a formula of the form I = a · e^{b·θ} (text: 'I=«9*e  *, where I = saturation current, a and b constants, and $ the absolute temperature').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report empirical formulae that summarise observed relations, state the domain of validity (temperatures tested) and the degree of fit ('fair accuracy').
